'''''Hydrocharis spongia''''', also known as '''''Limnobium spongia''''', and commonly known as the '''American frogbit''' or the '''American spongeplant''',<ref name=Flora>{{Cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=222000213|title=''Limnobium spongia'' in Flora of North America @ efloras.org|website=www.efloras.org|access-date=26 May 2025}}</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Hydrocharitaceae]].<ref name = powo/> It is native to the central and southeastern United States, where it grows in the Lower Mississippi Valley as far north as Illinois, and on the Southern Coastal Plain from Texas to Delaware.<ref name = powo/><ref name = Flora/> It is occasionally found elsewhere as a [[Waif#Botany|waif]].<ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Limnobium%20spongia.png Biota of North America Program, 2013 county distribution map] Image</ref> It grows in the slow-moving water of streams, bayous, and lakes from sea level up to 100 meters elevation.<ref name=Flora/>

== Description ==
The plants are herbaceous, growing up to 50 cm long. Heart-shaped or nearly rounded leaves are floating or emersed, 1–3 in (2–7 cm) in diameter. The leaves have two forms, often on the same plant. Floating leaves have a thick layer of spongy [[aerenchyma]] on the underside, while the emerged leaves lack the aerenchyma. Plants are mostly [[dioecy|dioecious]] and sometimes [[monoecy|monoecious]] and flower in summer and fall, mostly on plants with emersed leaves. Fruits are 4 to 12 mm diameter form from pistillate flowers, and once pollinated the peduncle becomes recurved to push the developing fruit below the water surface.<ref name = Flora/>

== Distribution ==
The native range of ''Hydrocharis spongia'' is predominantly the southeastern United States, with it specifically being present in: Texas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, and Connecticut. It is sometimes rare in the northeastern areas of its native range, such as Illinois.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Sponge Plant (Limnobium spongia) |url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/wetland/plants/sponge_plant.html |access-date=2026-04-26 |website=www.illinoiswildflowers.info}}</ref> Its preferred habitat include sloughs, ditches, swampy forests, in slow-moving or stagnant water with muddy substrate.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Limnobium spongia page |url=https://www.missouriplants.com/Limnobium_spongia_page.html |access-date=2026-04-26 |website=www.missouriplants.com}}</ref>

== Identification ==
[[File:Limnobium spongia 70276935.jpg|thumb|360x360px|Image showing signature whitish stems]]
''Hydrocharis spongia'' can be confused with ''Pontederia crassipes'' (formerly ''Eichhornia crassipes''), commonly known as the Common Water Hyacinth. They key feature to look out when determining the difference between the two is the root color. American Frogbit will have whitish roots and stems, whereas Common Water Hyacinth with have darkly colored roots and stems. Some other key features are that American Frogbit has ridged leaf stalks, and the undersides of young leaves have a central disk of red spongy cells, which helps to distinguish it from European Frogbit.<ref>{{Cite web |title={{!}} Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants {{!}} University of Florida, IFAS |url=https://plant-directory.ifas.ufl.edu/plant-directory/limnobium-spongia/ |access-date=2026-04-26 |website=plant-directory.ifas.ufl.edu}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
The roots of ''Hydrocharis spongia'' are known habitats for various zooplankton species to use in order to disperse their resting stages.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Battauz |first1=Yamila S. |last2=de Paggi |first2=Susana B. José |last3=Paggi |first3=Juan C. |date=June 2017 |title=Macrophytes as dispersal vectors of zooplankton resting stages in a subtropical riverine floodplain |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10452-016-9610-3 |journal=Aquatic Ecology |language=en |volume=51 |issue=2 |pages=191–201 |doi=10.1007/s10452-016-9610-3 |bibcode=2017AqEco..51..191B |hdl=11336/59819 |issn=1386-2588|hdl-access=free }}</ref> American Frogbit is also important habitat for various mosquito species, especially those in the genus ''Mansonia''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Saraiva |first1=José Ferreira |last2=Dos Santos Barroso |first2=Jéssica Fernanda |last3=Santos Neto |first3=Noel Fernandes |last4=Rabelo Furtado |first4=Nercy Virginia |last5=Carvalho |first5=Dario Pires |last6=Ribeiro |first6=Kaio Augusto |last7=Pereira Lima |first7=José Bento |last8=Galardo |first8=Allan Kardec Ribeiro |date=March 2023 |title=Oviposition Activity of Mansonia Species in Areas Along the Madeira River, Brazilian Amazon Rainforest |url=https://jamca.kglmeridian.com/view/journals/moco/39/1/article-p52.xml |journal=Journal of the American Mosquito Control Association |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=52–56 |doi=10.2987/22-7099 |pmid=37043604 |issn=1943-6270|doi-access=free }}</ref> One particularly infamous mosquito species is ''Anopheles quadrimaculatus'', also known as the Common Malaria Mosquito. The sugar in American Frog-bit is a known food source of the Common Malaria Mosquito, so a test was undertaken to determine if sugar traps with boric acid could be used with these plants along with two others that these mosquitoes also feed on the sugar of. The test ultimately concluded that American Frog-bit had performed the worst out of the three.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=BloreI BeierII XueIII |first=KaiI JohnII Rui-DeIII |date=March 2018 |title=Impact of Three Species of Aquatic Plants on Anopheles quadrimaculatus and its Effect on the Efficacy of Boric Acid Sugar Baits |journal=Journal of the American Mosquito Control Association |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=50–52 |doi=10.2987/17-6660.1 |pmid=31442109 |s2cid=90476224 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Environmental concerns ==
While ''Hydrocharis spongia'' is native to some parts of America, climate change can cause it and other members of its genus to spread beyond their native range, causing them to threaten the native aquatic plants in these new areas.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Jiongming |last2=Fu |first2=Zhihao |last3=Xiao |first3=Keyan |last4=Dong |first4=Hongjin |last5=Zhou |first5=Yadong |last6=Zhan |first6=Qinghua |date=2023-12-10 |title=Climate Change Potentially Leads to Habitat Expansion and Increases the Invasion Risk of Hydrocharis (Hydrocharitaceae) |journal=Plants |language=en |volume=12 |issue=24 |pages=4124 |doi=10.3390/plants12244124 |doi-access=free |issn=2223-7747 |pmc=10748102 |pmid=38140451 |bibcode=2023Plnts..12.4124Y }}</ref> Additionally, American Frog-bit can cause negative ecological, social, and economic impacts that can harm aquatic fauna (i.e., dissolved oxygen depletion) and restrict human uses of water when it is allowed to grow extensively. This is because American Frog-bit can form large, extensive mats, which can grow out of control if they aren’t kept in check, encouraging the use of herbicides in areas where it is spreading.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Turnage |first1=Gray |last2=Lazaro-Lobo |first2=Adrian |last3=Blassingame |first3=Ben |last4=Robinson |first4=Olivia |last5=Calhoun |first5=Kennedy |last6=Ervin |first6=Gary |date=2023-01-01 |title=American frogbit response to herbicides |url=https://apms.org/journal/ |journal=Journal of Aquatic Plant Management |volume=61 |doi=10.57257/JAPM-D-21-00022 |bibcode=2023JAqPM..61.....T |url-access=subscription }}</ref> This is rather concerning, since climate change in the American southeast has been increasing temperatures in the region by about 2°F since 1970.<ref>{{Cite web |last=US EPA |first=OA |title=Climate Impacts in the Southeast |url=https://19january2017snapshot.epa.gov/climate-impacts/climate-impacts-southeast |access-date=2026-04-26 |website=19january2017snapshot.epa.gov |language=en}}</ref>

== Cultivation and usage ==
The primary use for cultivating ''Hydrocharis spongia'' is to provide shade for fish or other aquatic fauna in domestic tanks, ponds, or pools. American Frog-bit prefers full sun, and blooms during the summer.<ref>{{Cite web |title=American Frogbit (Limnobium spongia) - MyGardenLife |url=https://mygardenlife.com/plant-library/american-frogbit-limnobium-spongia |access-date=2026-04-26 |language=en-US}}</ref> Stagnant or slow-moving water is preferred, and it can spread aggressively in areas with warm climates. A fungal disease, known as ''Cercospora limnobii'', can cause brown lesions to develop on the leaf blades.<ref name=":0" />
